Rule hierarchy · which instruction wins?

Higher rules take priority. Targets are flexible.

1 · Non-negotiable safeguards

Follow the official exam instructions, assigned time and invigilator directions. Save deliberately, check the asked value and answer format, clear unintentional MCQs, verify necessary premises, and protect a final response audit. Never let a score target justify violating these safeguards.

2 · Adaptive checkpoints

VARC: 45–60s passage gate, 45s unresolved two-option deadlock. DILR: reassess , switch by if stalled. QA: ignition, about in R1 and in R2. Continue briefly only for a credible imminent payoff; otherwise move on. Protect the remaining section time.

3 · Strong default execution plans

Use the selected VARC mode, four-minute DILR scan, one reliable set then a second viable set, and QA rolling triage. The 40-minute clocks, attempt ranges and operating scenarios are planning guides; rebase them after a switch or unexpected difficulty. Never force completion.

4 · Personal preferences and tie-breakers

Prefer coded or elimination-driven DILR only when equally viable; prefer your strongest QA topics, but take any obvious sitter. Prefer paper for simple calculation, calculator when faster or safer. Choose the fourth RC only under its specific trigger, not because a quota calls for it.

Conflict examples: a productive DILR breakthrough can override the nominal set duration, not the section deadline. An easy geometry sitter can override topic preference, not verification. A weak TITA or 50/50 MCQ must not displace a more reliable answer; use cleanup only after safer work. A poor earlier section never changes the next section's marking or clock.

CAT 2026 · examination logistics

Reviewed 26 Nov 2026

Sunday, 29 November 2026. IIM Indore's releases dated 26 July and 4 November announce three sessions and a standard 120-minute paper with 40 minutes per section, in VARC → DILR → QA order, without switching sections. Follow your approved accommodations and actual on-screen instructions if different. The question mix and marks shown elsewhere are planning assumptions, not a guaranteed blueprint.

Your admit card is authoritative: confirm the exact date, shift, centre address, reporting time and gate-closing time on your own card. The gate deadline is not the examination start. Aim to arrive by reporting time or earlier, not just before gate closure. Do not rely on admission after the stated gate deadline.

By Saturday, 28 November

  • Verify the actual centre, entrance and route (visit if practical); plan transport, backup ride, parking/walking and queue time. Target arrival before reporting; departure = target arrival minus realistic journey time and contingency (for example, 30–60 minutes extra if traffic is uncertain).

On Sunday · before leaving

  • Recheck portal updates, admit card, ID, route and the departure deadline. Allow extra time for security and identity checks; the 4 November release describes face matching and jammers at selected centres.

Follow centre-specific clothing restrictions, including reported guidance on thick soles and large buttons. Ask officials about any required medical device or religious accommodation in advance.

02. VARC — 3 RCs + 8 VA strategy

Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension (VARC) · recent pattern: 24 questions / 40 minutes

3 RCs + 8 VA strategy (17–18 attempts)

Illustrative score calculation Illustrative: 17–18 attempts, 13–14 correct, 2 wrong MCQs and 2 wrong TITAs = 37–40 raw marks. Each correct-to-wrong MCQ swing costs 4 marks. Accuracy first; do not force attempts.
Standard (3 RCs): 3 RCs → 4 TITA VA → 4 MCQ VA → 1m Cleanup 20-Q Active Pool
Reading comprehensionStructural reading, evidence checks and option elimination

RC: read for structure, then check evidence

~8m / RC

Why Neither Extreme Works

Avoid Fast Scan + Jump to Qs Without a mental map, you must reread whole paragraphs.
Avoid refusing to reread Unrealistic for CAT; traps hinge on single qualifiers (mostly vs. solely, correlates vs. causes).
1

First paragraph: decide in 45–60s

Do not compare every passage upfront. Judge the first paragraph by comprehension, not topic. If you cannot state its point after 45–60 seconds, move on; reject more than one if necessary. Default to three readable passages. If two passages fail the gate, protect the most readable remaining RCs and shift freed time to viable VA; do not force a third or fourth passage to meet a target.

2

Pass 1 (3:00–3:30) — Architecture, Not Facts

  • Steady normal-to-brisk pace. Default No-Backtracking Rule on confusing lines: the next sentence may clarify the meaning; briefly reread only if the argument cannot otherwise be followed.
  • Do not memorise names, dates or secondary examples; register where they appear for targeted verification.
  • Tag each paragraph's role in 3–5 words (Old view → Critique → Evidence → Caveat).
  • Read deliberately at pivot words that signal argumentative shifts: however, yet, ironically, although, despite, rather, paradoxically, admittedly, consequently.
3

Answering (4:00–4:30) — Split by Question Type

  • Global Qs (Main Idea / Tone / Purpose / Structure): answer from the mental map first; verify selectively if needed. Practice diagnostic: extensive rereading for the main idea suggests the initial structural read needs improvement.
  • Specific / EXCEPT: locate relevant evidence, check alternatives for EXCEPT, and read enough context to verify the qualifier. Inference: use local evidence where sufficient; otherwise combine premises across paragraphs and distinguish what follows from what is merely plausible. A 15–20s lookup is a guide, not a limit on understanding.
  • Never force 4/4 on a passage; 3/4 can be preferable if one inference trap is nasty.

45s Two-Option Deadlock

4-Point Checklist

Two options left? Check these four traps:

  1. 01 Extreme / Scope Shift: Uses only, always, never, solely, completely when the author is cautious (tends to, often, primarily).
  2. 02 True outside the passage, unsupported inside: May be true in real life, but the passage does not support it.
  3. 03 Changed meaning, tone or cause: correlates ≠ causes; flips cause/effect; confuses critic vs. author; or mismatches tone (e.g., hostile/dismissive option when author is mildly skeptical).
  4. 04 Half-Right Trap: One half is supported; the other is not.
Deadlock checkpoint 45s → stop deliberating; flag unanswered

In cleanup, first save penalty-free TITA answers and any clearer opportunities. Revisit genuinely shortlisted MCQs only if time remains; if two options really are equally likely, the expected raw score is +1 (0.5 × 3 − 0.5 × 1). This is not a guarantee. If elimination is unreliable or sectional accuracy is at risk, leave blank. Clear any speculative saved MCQ before moving on unless deliberately committing to it.

Verbal ability techniquesSummary, completion, odd sentence and para jumbles

The 4 VA Playbooks

Checkpoint: ~2:00 / question
VA risk and opportunity — personal hypotheses Compare your accuracy
1. Possible strengths

Para Summary & Para Completion (MCQs) — Para Completion gives an ordered paragraph. Test your accuracy in mocks.

2. No negative marking

Odd One Out (TITA, 0 penalty) — find the sentence that breaks the paragraph's focus; no exact order needed.

3. Exact sequence

Para Jumbles (TITA, 0 penalty) — all-or-nothing (flipping 1 pair like 2413 vs 2143 = 0); prioritise viable questions with an approximate 2:00 checkpoint; a wrong answer earns no marks under the recent pattern.

1. Para Summary

MCQ -1 Structural anchors
  • Method: Read the paragraph once like a miniature RC, then state Subject + Core Claim + Contrast/Condition mentally before viewing options.
  • Trigger: Preserve both sides of any pivot word (however, yet, although).
  • Trap: An option focuses on an example, drops a qualification or adds an outside opinion.

2. Para Completion

MCQ -1 Structural anchors
  • Method: Read the missing sentence FIRST for links to earlier text (this, such, they, however, instead) and links to what follows.
  • Trigger: Find the gap. Check both links: [Before] + [Insert] + [After].
  • Trap: Fits the previous sentence but breaks the next sentence's logic or pronouns.

3. Odd Sentence Out

TITA 0 Penalty-free opportunity
  • Method: Build the 4-sentence coherent paragraph first (find 3 sharing exact subject + angle).
  • Trigger: Separate Topic from Scope; sanity-check by sequencing the remaining 4 lines.
  • Trap: Lexical Decoys — shared buzzwords planted in the odd line to disguise a scope drift.

4. Para Jumbles

TITA 0 Time checkpoint
  • Method: Find sentence pairs that must go together before choosing the opener.
  • Triggers: Noun → Pronoun, Cause → Effect, Claim → Contrast, General → Example, Full form → Acronym, Earlier → Later (chronology). Test each pair against the whole paragraph.
  • Checkpoint: Around 2:00, move on if stalled. Save a defensible sequence if actual marking is penalty-free; otherwise judge confidence and opportunity cost. Revisit a reasonable estimate only in cleanup after stronger opportunities.

03. DILR — Set selection and solving

Data Interpretation and Logical Reasoning (DILR) · recent pattern: 5 sets / 22 questions / 40 minutes

One reliable set → two viable sets; optional extra questions

Target: =
·
·
·
· Rebase after a switch.
Equal difficulty? Choose five questions If a 5-Q set and a 4-Q set look equally clean in your scan, pick the 5-Q set first (+3 extra marks if the additional question is solved correctly for comparable overall effort).
When to use the calculator Use paper for simple sums and ratios; use the permitted calculator whenever faster or more reliable.
General set-selection flagsRepresentation, anchors, casework and calculation burden

Green Flags (Pick Early)

Min 0–4 Scan
  • + Clear data structure: Obvious grid, matrix, Venn diagram, or timeline.
  • + Useful starting facts: Fixed numbers, exact positions, or a total/bound that quickly forces a value.
  • + Favorable question stems: Exact values or conditional stems ("If X = 5...").
  • + Familiar formats: 2D/3D Tables, Tournaments, Venn, quantitative reasoning, linear/circular arrangements, and bar/line charts combined with logical constraints.

Red Flags (Skip / Leave Last)

Avoid Early
  • × Dense text with no useful representation or stated/derivable anchor; length alone is not decisive.
  • × Too many cases: Many early independent branches without useful pruning.
  • × Heavy calculation burden: several difficult computations without simplification, or genuinely ambiguous constraints.
  • × Potentially slow questions: Many "Min/Max" or "CANNOT be true" questions. Such questions can still be favourable when bounds or elimination are tractable.
Caution: Don't auto-pick missing-cell tables just because they look like data interpretation.

Personal set-selection filter

Your stated preference is for constrained, coded-response reasoning rather than open positional casework or weak aggregate clues. Treat it as a starting hypothesis, not a proven advantage: choose the set with the best actual route to marks.

Prefer when the clues are strong

  • Binary, yes/no or coded responses with clear meanings and restrictive totals.
  • Interdependent constraints that force elimination, chaining or a bounded case split.
  • Concrete placements, exact values or easily derivable anchors (totals, parity, bounds).
  • Intermediate states you can determine and verify without enumerating every possibility.
  • A central breakthrough you can plausibly reach, with linked or independently answerable questions.

Avoid when cases are hard to narrow

  • Positional arrangements with many independent choices and little pruning.
  • Weakly constrained aggregates without a useful total, bound or cross-link.
  • Calculation-heavy missing tables, especially with several unknowns per relation.
  • Exhaustive enumeration or several competing cases with no obvious elimination.
  • Do not reject a genre automatically: a tight arrangement or aggregate set may be easier than a poorly constrained coded set.

During the 0–4 minute scan

Scan every available set. For each, ask: Can I represent it? What is directly given, and what anchor can be derived by totals, bounds or chaining? Which deduction unlocks the central constraint, and how long might it take? How many branches or calculations remain, and what questions pay off before a full solve?

Rank by credible time to reliable answers, not passage length, topic familiarity or raw constraint count. Use the personal preference as a tie-breaker; prefer a five-question set over a four-question set only when overall effort and risk are comparable. After , reassess actual progress; switch by if stalled.

Calibration: in the error log, record the set chosen, the reason, first useful deduction, time and independent correctness. Compare this with alternatives before strengthening or reversing your preference.

The 6-Minute Bail-Out Rule

checkpoint

Stay only if: A central constraint is unlocked, or meaningful deductions are accumulating with a credible route to answerable questions.

Bail immediately if: You have no useful representation or new deduction, are circularly rereading, or a better ranked set has a more credible route. Reassess at ; switch by if still stalled.

Check before answering

ERROR-LOG TRIGGERS
  1. 1 20–60s Clue Back-Check: Check relevant constraints, totals and feasibility. Confirm uniqueness of the requested answer across surviving cases (the full grid need not be unique). Re-read the exact quantity and units asked. For independent partial questions, verify necessary premises and answer without waiting for a complete grid.
  2. 2 Write important totals: Record consequential intermediate totals, bounds and integer restrictions; independently cross-check vulnerable sums. Use the permitted calculator if it reduces time or error.

Case discipline: master model vs hypothetical question

Keep stated facts and necessary deductions in the master model. Label uncertain branches A/B; an "if" condition belongs in a separate temporary copy or clearly marked overlay. Never carry a question-specific assumption into the next question. Eliminate infeasible branches using the original clues, totals, bounds and integrality. If valid cases remain, test whether the asked value agrees in all of them; for possible/minimum/maximum questions, check the requested feasibility or bound instead of demanding uniqueness.

DILR failure recovery · reset the clock, not the goal

Elapsed minutes; examples assume an early checkpoint switch and roughly per viable set. Do not force two sets if the remaining time or paper does not support them.

A · First set stalls

Preserve any independently verified answers and switch promptly.

B · Second set stalls

Preserve saved, verified first-set answers; do not chase the failed set.

Late failure / both stall: recalculate remaining minutes after reserving the last minute. Prefer independently answerable questions or a partly solved set with a credible breakthrough. If no complete set is feasible, protect reliable partial marks and reasoned TITA entries. Never invent a full solution to meet a target.

Representation referenceFive recurring reasoning structures

Choose a useful diagram or table

5 High-Yield Archetypes
01Mapping / Distribution Put the fixed entity (Days, Ranks, Slots, Teams) on rows/columns; never map floating variables against floating variables.
02Games & Tournaments Draw an upper-triangle match matrix + Points summary; compute total matches = n(n-1)/2 for a complete single round-robin. Derive total points from scoring rules (fixed points per match × matches, or separate win/draw totals when variable).
03Quant-Based Reasoning Write row/column total equations first; check parity (odd/even), divisibility, and min/max bounds.
04Venn Diagrams Label all 7 (or 15) atomic regions with variables (a, b, c...) before plugging in any clues.
05Routes & Networks Redraw messy diagrams cleanly with directional arrows and explicit node capacities / costs.

04. QA — Question selection and solving

Quantitative Ability (QA) · recent pattern: 22 questions / 40 minutes

Build toward answers ()

Recent-paper estimates: Arithmetic 7–9 and Algebra 4–8 questions depending on slot and classification; Number System may offer additional opportunities. Verify actual counts and marking on exam day.

Assess questions as you go
ROUND 1 ·

ROUND 2 ·

ROUND 3 · Optional extra + TITA sweep

QA skip routing · classify once, revisit selectively

Keep the rolling triage; no separate full-paper scan. At minute 22, if questions remain unseen, continue first-pass triage before revisiting L/I, so easy unseen questions are not lost. Aim to assess every question before minute 36 without sacrificing a near-complete answer or the cleanup reserve. Use question numbers on the rough sheet only if useful; the exam palette remains your navigation aid.

Skip classSignalAction
L · Solvable but lengthy
Clear method, more steps than R1 allows.
Mark unanswered for review. R2 high priority.
I · Calculation incomplete
Known method and useful working already on paper.
Mark unanswered for review. R2 high priority; finish first if near completion.
U · Method uncertain
Possible route, but no reliable setup.
Low priority; mark only if there is a credible avenue. Revisit after L/I.
X · Conceptual gap / unfamiliar geometry
No meaningful route or requires a technique you do not know.
Leave unanswered and unflagged; do not revisit for full solving.
T · Unsolved TITA
Type-in-the-answer question, incomplete solution.
In cleanup consider a reasoned estimate if penalty-free. T is an overlay, not a reason to spend extra solving time.

Round 2: finish first-pass assessment of unseen questions, then prioritise L/I by confidence and remaining minutes to finish; U only after stronger opportunities. Round 3: save/audit responses, protect TITA opportunities and attempt an extra question only if time remains. Clear uncertain saved MCQ responses before marking for review.

Quantitative execution rulesIgnition, arithmetic, geometry, algebra and verification

Six rules for solving QA

Execution Discipline
01

ignition & checkpoint

By , identify a definite method, equation, ratio or conceptual route. If none, classify U/X and move on. In R1, reassess at ; briefly extend only if completion is imminent. Mark L/I or genuinely viable U for review; leave dead skips unflagged.

02

Do not skip arithmetic by length

"Pen-Down on Word One": Force yourself to read the first 2 lines of every Arithmetic problem in Round 1 before deciding to skip; write meaningful variables, ratios, timelines and constraints as you read. Length alone is neither a green nor a red flag; do not auto-reject Arithmetic because it looks long.

03

Geometry: take easy questions

Personal default: quickly defer complex geometry, circle theorems or angle chasing if no obvious route. Allow direct mensuration and obvious similarity, Pythagoras or circle-basics sitters. Classify L/I/U/X by actual method, not topic alone.

04

Algebra Speed Discipline

Rely on muscle memory (arithmetic/geometric progressions, Linear/Quadratics). Only use value plug-in (n=1,2 or x=0,1,-1) or test option boundaries in inequalities (respect the domain and strict/non-strict endpoints), if the technique clicks naturally within 15s — don't force new habits last week.

05

Final answer audit (about 15 seconds)

Before saving deliberately via the verified interface, re-read the requested value (often the last 8–10 words), unit, sign, domain and answer format. Silly errors happen at the finish line — catch x vs 2x, "time taken by B alone", or "% more than" before losing 4 marks.

06

When to use the calculator

Paper for simple sums and ratios. Use the on-screen calculator when faster or safer: difficult division, powers or totals. Routine calculator use can waste time.
